title: Watch Night
subtitle: The Bronx, Midtown and Harlem, New York
focus: Everything in one night: Hip Hop elders meeting the soul elders they looped, arena pop spectacle, and the root of it all: the Watch Night service, the watchman's lantern, call and response

intro.t: December thirtieth. The Bronx. Breath showing, coats zipped to the chin, and the lamppost on the corner humming like it remembers May.
Back where they first played me twice.
Cross's speaker boxes, the ones his father built, stand against the park fence under a blue tarp. The cable runs up the lamppost like ivy. In forty years nobody from the city has ever asked.
For the record, that is still technically illegal.
The old crews are coming in out of the cold. Sixties and seventies, good coats and old sneakers, carrying crates of records the way other people carry casseroles.
Word went round: the drummer is coming. The one they looped for fifty years without knowing his name. They came to look at his hands.
Listen. In May I had a reel and a hunch. Tonight I got the man himself, and a better extension cord.
Gloves come off for the records, Pocket. Hands go in your pockets in between. That's the whole science.
Tomorrow night I get sold, or I don't. Tonight, at least, it's cold enough to see everybody breathing.

gigs.title: Coats On
gigs.blurb: The park jam in December: breath showing, power from the lamppost, and the drummer they looped standing by the turntables.

vibe.label: Old-school hip hop and the breaks it came from

challenge.text: Looped by the best: 870 notes in a row, ten times the tempo.

before.t: Deacon arrives in a borrowed parka zipped to the chin, sticks in the breast pocket anyway. The crowd opens a path for him without anybody saying to.
An old man in a sheepskin coat, who had this park on Saturday nights when Cross was a boy, takes off one glove to shake his hand, and does not let go for a while.
Deacon. On behalf of every crew that ever plugged into that lamppost: we looped you because we couldn't afford a drummer that good.
Son, in 1967 neither could the man who hired me.
The whole park laughs, and the steam of it hangs over the turntables like a cloud with good timing.
So this is where it happened. Two machines, one cable from a lamppost, and nobody holding the tempo.
Professor, I held that tempo with my thumb for forty years.
Then your thumb has been rushing since 1977.
Move over, baby. I want a turn. Show me how you make it go backwards. I want to try it on Wendell.
Before anybody touches anything: your ground's bad, Cross. Daddy would've fixed this in 1977. Hand me that tape.
Pocket. Cold hands play late. Keep them in your pockets till you need them.
Yes, Nana.
Ren tapes the ground. The lamppost hums a little prouder. One, two... one, two, three, four.

afterWin.t: A park jam in December is a park jam with steam coming off it. Coats came off by the second song. Hats did not. Some things are sacred.
Then Cross lifts the reel out of Tuesday's tote, threads it with his gloves off, and the lamppost hums the way it did in May.
One more time for the park. Last time it played here, nobody knew who was talking.
The voices come out of the speaker boxes. And this time, the voices are standing in front of them.
'Deacon.' Two voices, sixty years apart. 'Low.' Ren, with her father, on the beat. 'Sister.' Ruth, laughing already. 'Professor.' Exactly on time, both of him.
Then the laugh. The nineteen-year-old on the tape laughs, and the seventy-nine-year-old in the red jacket laughs with her. And then they both say it.
...Dess.
Four bars. Then the tape runs out, the way it always does, and the park makes a sound I have never once heard a park make.
Mm-hm.
Tomorrow's Watch Night. Wendell. Ruth. Aurelius. Ren, baby. Bring your red jackets.
Dess, I don't own a red jacket.
You will by morning.

afterLose.t: Cold hands. Happens. Lamppost's still on. Again.
They kept me going on two copies for forty years. You can keep going one more time. Run it back.

gigs.title: Watch Night 60
gigs.blurb: You open the biggest night in Lantern's history. The headliner is made of light. Nobody looks at the usher.

vibe.label: Arena pop and R&B, everything at once

challenge.text: Carry the arena to midnight: earn 18 stars over the set.

before.sub: Watch Night 60, Midtown Arena. You open. Twenty thousand people clap the way people clap for weather.

before.t: Tell Mr. Ellery I won't be joining his finale, darling. I don't duet with anything I can walk through.

At the staff door, Bryce Whitlock holds a list of five names who are not to enter the building. Five ushers in red jackets come in out of the cold, flashlights pointed at the floor, the way ushers do.
Watch your step.
He does not look up. Nobody looks at the usher.
The Birthrights play their set, clean as glass. Then, at 11:31, the arena goes dark for the headliner.
Ladies and gentlemen. The band that never has to stop. The Lark Five: Forever.
Five figures made of light. They play me perfectly, every note exactly where it was in 1967. Not one of them was ever nineteen.

Then, at the back of the arena, five flashlights come on and start down five aisles toward the five figures. Twenty thousand people turn around to look at the ushers. Kingston walks to the edge of the stage and kneels.
Mrs. Fontaine. I believe this is yours.
She takes his microphone. She sings three of the five notes. Then she stops, and leaves the rest of the bar open.
The hologram plays on. It cannot hear. Twenty thousand people sing the last two notes for her.
That is the difference between a record and a room. The room answers.

At the signing table, Vivienne Lark puts the pen down. She carries the contract to the edge of the stage and hands it down to Mrs. Fontaine, who tears it neatly in half, like a ticket, and hands Ellery his half.
Enjoy the show.
Fun fact.
Nobody interrupts. She is standing at the hologram console in the wings, in white cotton gloves, and twenty thousand people wait for her to finish.
It has an off switch.
Kingston crosses the stage and switches it off. Five figures go out like birthday candles. And page forty-one, clause three, says that at every show the Opening Act may introduce the band.
Miss Lark. Would you introduce the band?
Lantern Records has an error in its catalogue. Number L-1167, side B. We regret the error. It has taken us sixty years to regret it properly.
Wendell Arceneaux.
Here.
Lemuel Castile.
Here, for him.
Ruth Pettis.
Here.
Aurelius Finch.
Here.
Odessa Fontaine.
Here.
That is an admission, on a stage, in front of twenty thousand witnesses. That one was free.
{band}. Take them to midnight.

afterWin.t: Twenty thousand people counted down from ten over the top of your closer, and a few blocks away the ball dropped right on your downbeat. I could not have timed it better. I did not time it at all.
Midnight. The window shuts. The pen is still lying where Vivienne Lark put it down.
There's no asset here.
He tucks the tablet under his arm and walks off the side of the stage. Nobody stops him. Nobody watches him go. The sale is dead.
Asset tally: three. Final entry: zero. I'm underlining it.
Mrs. Fontaine.
Miss Lark.
Then the arena empties onto the avenue and, without anybody saying so, turns north. Twenty thousand people in paper hats, walking uptown in the cold. Some take the train. Some take a church van.
Text from Harlem. No words. Just a picture.
The theater doors, propped wide open with a push broom.
Happy New Year, Nana.
Not yet, baby. Not till we get uptown.

afterLose.t: They'll wait, baby. Twenty thousand people, and not one of them's going home.
Midnight can wait one more song. I've waited sixty years. Run it back.

gigs.title: Watch Night
gigs.blurb: Twelve-thirty in the morning. Mr. Broom has kept the doors open, and the stairs are where they have always been.

vibe.label: Everything that came from the church and went back to it

challenge.text: Watch your step: one song with no misses.

before.t: The marquee is lit. Somebody climbed a ladder at a quarter to midnight and changed the letters: {band}. And underneath, smaller, in Mr. Broom's careful capitals: (MT. NEBO YOUTH CHOIR).
Well. That's what was parked out front.
The line goes round the block, and it is three lines braided into one.
The Greater Hope congregation from two blocks over, still in their church clothes, straight from the midnight shout. The park crowd from the Bronx, in coats that smell like the lamppost.
And the arena crowd in paper hats, who walked sixty blocks uptown in the cold and would like everybody to know it.
Inside, the house fills to the back wall. In row Z, Tuesday has saved one seat with her tote bag and a look.
Nana Dess comes in by the side door in her red jacket. She unhooks the brass flashlight, clicks it on, and walks straight to aisle three. Forty years of habit.
Then she stops.
Nana. Over here. Row Z. I bought you a ticket. A paying customer's seat.
Odessa looks at the ticket a long time. She does not tear it.
Well. Never had one of these.
She clicks the flashlight off and sits down in row Z, next to Tuesday. Forty years in this house, and it is the first time she has sat down in it.
Backstage, Mr. Broom takes a key on a string from his vest pocket and unlocks the stage door. He says nothing. He holds it open.
{band}. I don't know how tonight ends.
Neither do we.
Good. I think that's good.
Last set, Pocket. Longest one. Take your time. Nobody's selling it tonight.

afterWin.t: The house is on its feet. It has been since somewhere in the third song, and it has decided, all of it together, not to sit back down.
The church crowd claps on two and four. The park crowd claps on two and four. The arena crowd has caught on, and nobody is going to tell them they were late.
By the wings, Mr. Broom leans on his broom, unused. He has not swept anybody off tonight. He does not look like a man planning to start.
Nana. You're standing up.
Whole house is standing, baby. I'm just part of the house.
In the wings, four people in red jackets with nothing left to usher are standing very still.
They want one more.
Pocket. That next one ain't yours.

afterLose.t: Doors stay open all night tonight.
I have been played wrong by the best, in this very room. Run it back.

afterChallenge.t: 1:04 a.m., Watch Night, 1967. The sidewalk outside Lantern. Snow coming down slow, the kind that only sticks to hats.
The Professor waited until the brownstone door had shut behind them. Then he took the original reel out of his overcoat, where it had ridden since the control room.
He gave it to Dess. 'Somebody keep it.' He did not say why it should be her, and nobody asked.
She had no pen. Low had a blue ballpoint clipped inside his ledger. He handed it over without being asked.
She wrote on the lid of the box against the iron railing, in capitals nobody could misread: WATCH NIGHT - 11 SEC - DO NOT ERASE.
Ruth said Happy New Year first. Deacon shook every hand, one at a time. The Professor said it to the snow.
Then they walked five ways home, and by morning the snow had filled in all five sets of footprints.
Nobody said anything about bar five. There wasn't any tape left.
